desc:
A non-decreasing array (repeated values allowed) was cut at some position into a front part and a back part and the two parts were swapped, producing nums. For example [1, 3, 3] may become [3, 3, 1] or [3, 1, 3], and [2, 2, 2, 0, 1] comes from [0, 1, 2, 2, 2]. A cut at the very start or end leaves the array as it is.

Return the smallest value in nums. Do better than a plain scan whenever the duplicates allow it, and explain what the worst case is.
constraints: nums is a rotation of a non-decreasing array
hints: The classic search compares nums[mid] with nums[hi]. When values are distinct this decides the side every time. Which comparison outcome becomes ambiguous with duplicates?
If nums[mid] > nums[hi] the minimum is right of mid; if nums[mid] < nums[hi] it is at mid or left. Only nums[mid] == nums[hi] is unclear: the minimum may be on either side.
In the tie case you can safely discard just hi: its value is repeated at mid, so if hi held the minimum, mid still holds that same minimum. Do hi -= 1 and continue.
editorial: Keep a window [lo, hi] that always contains a copy of the minimum. If nums[mid] > nums[hi], the 'cliff' where values drop is right of mid, so mid cannot be the minimum: lo = mid + 1. If nums[mid] < nums[hi], the segment from mid to hi is increasing, so the minimum is at mid or earlier: hi = mid.

With nums[mid] == nums[hi] nothing is known about the sides: [1, 1, 1, 0, 1] and [1, 0, 1, 1, 1] both have this tie at the first step, yet the minimum lies on opposite sides. What can be said is that removing hi never loses the minimum value, because an equal value stays at mid. So shrink with hi -= 1.

Each tie costs one element, so the worst case is O(n) (an array of all equal values with one smaller value hidden somewhere shows that no algorithm can do better: that single value could be at any index and each comparison reveals at most one position). On inputs with few ties it is O(log n). Space O(1).
